item.title: The Evening Protocol: Engineering the Conditions for Deep Sleep
item.author: hello@offdaycollective.com (Off Day Collective)
item.dc:creator: Off Day Collective
item.description: Sleep is not the absence of wakefulness. It is an active biological process — and the evening is where it is either enabled or compromised. The glymphatic system, melatonin action spectra, temperature regulation, and the real cost of one late drink.
item.content:encoded:
Sleep is not the absence of wakefulness. It is an active biological process — and the evening is where it is either enabled or compromised.

In this article: the glymphatic system (Xie et al., 2013), why 480nm blue light suppresses melatonin at a 10-lux threshold (Brainard et al., 2001), how a warm bath accelerates sleep onset via peripheral vasodilation (Kräuchi et al., 1999), and the mechanism by which even moderate alcohol suppresses REM sleep by up to 24%.

item.title: The Art of Strategic Idling: How Doing Nothing Produces Your Best Work
item.author: hello@offdaycollective.com (Off Day Collective)
item.dc:creator: Off Day Collective
item.description: Creativity does not arrive at a desk. It arrives in the shower, on a walk, in the quiet moment between two tasks. The Default Mode Network, the 90-minute BRAC rhythm, and why a Stanford study found walking boosts creative output by 81%.
item.content:encoded:
Creativity does not arrive at a desk. It arrives in the shower, on a walk, in the quiet moment between two tasks. Your brain's most generative state is not focus — it is the absence of it.

In this article: the Default Mode Network and what it actually does during rest (Buckner et al., 2008), Kleitman's 90-minute Basic Rest-Activity Cycle, Peretz Lavie's sleep gate research, and the Oppezzo & Schwartz walking study showing an 81% boost in divergent thinking.

item.title: The 90-Minute Window: Why Your First Hour Determines Your Entire Day
item.author: hello@offdaycollective.com (Off Day Collective)
item.dc:creator: Off Day Collective
item.description: Your body already knows how to wake up. Most morning routines spend the first 45 minutes overriding it. A peer-reviewed look at the cortisol awakening response, the danger of phone use in the first 30 minutes, caffeine timing, and light as a biological anchor.
item.content:encoded:
Your body already knows how to wake up. Most morning routines spend the first 45 minutes overriding it.

In this article: the Cortisol Awakening Response and why cortisol peaks 30–45 minutes after waking (Clow et al., 2004), how morning phone use triggers a threat-detection cascade, the adenosine-caffeine competition and why waiting 90 minutes produces a cleaner response (Porkka-Heiskanen, 1999), and light exposure as the master signal for your circadian clock (Czeisler et al., 1999).
